cues.text: A Knight's Demand
On Holy Thursday, 1384 — traditionally dated to March 25, though scholars have noted Holy Thursday actually fell later that year — a knight named Oswald Milser arrived at Mass.
He was administrator of the nearby castle of Schlossberg and came armed with his men to the parish church of St. Oswald in Seefeld , in the Tyrol.
He demanded the large Host ordinarily reserved for the celebrating priest rather than the smaller Host given to the rest of the congregation.
The Ground Gives Way
The intimidated priest complied, and Milser received the oversized Host standing rather than kneeling.
The moment it touched his tongue, tradition holds, the stone floor beneath him began to tremble and give way.
Milser, sinking as if into quicksand, grasped desperately at the altar for support.
Blood Restored to the Altar
Only when the priest removed the Host from Milser's mouth did the trembling stop, and the ground steady itself again.
Blood, the account holds, then began flowing visibly from the Host itself, in full view of the terrified knight and the witnesses gathered for Mass.
What the Historical Record Actually Shows

A source-critical study published by a researcher at the University of Innsbruck's Institute for Practical Theology has established that contemporary records confirm only Oswald Milser's administrative office at Seefeld in 1384.
They also confirm that he lived until 1398, not 1386 as later legend claimed.
The study concludes that the fuller miracle narrative was likely constructed no earlier than the late fifteenth century and projected back onto the traditional 1384 date.
This entry follows that more cautious historical assessment rather than presenting every narrative detail as contemporaneous fact.
Legacy
Whatever the precise history behind its origin, devotion to the relic grew rapidly.
A hostel had to be built for the pilgrims who came, Duke Friedrich IV commissioned a larger church in 1423, and Emperor Maximilian I himself became a devoted patron of the site.
The Church of St. Oswald in Seefeld still displays the blood-stained Host in its reliquary today, along with the hollow in the floor.
The hollow is now covered by a protective grate, where tradition holds an arrogant knight's demand for special treatment was answered with a floor that would not hold him.
